SpaceX's Mars Colonial Transporter: What do we Know so Far?

It's real life Sheldon...

Good compilation of information though.

An 'affordable' trip to Mars doesn't make for an affordable lifestyle there. What are a million people supposed to do to earn a living on Mars and justify the very costly construction of their settlements, life support, and ISRU infrastructure? Government isn't in the business of inventing places for people to go and not pay taxes. They have no incentive or rationale for space settlement. Their only practical purpose for going to space today is to do Big Science. So don't expect anything better than a few temporary outposts housing elite astronauts. There's very little, if anything, on Mars that could realize an ROI on Wall Street. Asteroids offer the only slim hope of resource exploitation for Earth's benefit. So what do you pay back the bankers with? Government and capitalism are the only two ways our culture currently knows how to do Big Things and neither of them have any reason to do space settlement. So, again, what are a million people supposed to do there?

Space cadets will tell you about the inherent human compulsion to explore, the need for frontiers, and so on. They'll borrow moving rhetoric from Carl Sagan, Neil Degrasse Tyson, and Robert Zubrin. And that might be quite valid, but it means absolutely nothing to the people who write the checks in our culture right now. Government can't do things that don't somehow, matter to the lowest common denominator of a very big society--and the bigger the society the smaller the spectrum of those common interests. And, spending other people's money, they're required to, at least, pretend to do everything cost-efficiently. Space settlement is an interest chiefly of a small segment of a predominantly white and male, upper-middle-class, western cultural demographic composed of people unusually high up on Maslow's Pyramid. If you want a large society that cares about space, you better be pushing as many people up Maslow's Pyramid as possible--and our culture has lately been doing the exact opposite.

Business can't do anything that doesn't have a concrete ROI and it must always do it in the most cost-effective way. If robots run by AI can do the job for less, they win, end of story. There's a lot of denial about robotics and AI among space buffs, but it's still coming. EVA was never practical and no matter how cheap you make human space travel it can't be cheaper than AI's traveling by telecommunications.

So if we want to go live in space there needs to be another, third, way of doing Big Things that allows it to be justified emotionally, philosophically, or aesthetically rather than economically.

No matter how cheap the trip, personal homesteading on Mars is not in the near-term cards. Even the oligarch space cadets aren't rich enough to pull that off. If that's your hope or expectation, you better plan on becoming transhuman with a robust nanotechnology at-hand. But more near-term it might, just, be possible to pull-off 'community-steading'. But that implies that our Third Way of doing things is through intentional community. Essentially, making space development and settlement a very big community hobby project, like Linux or one of those 'fly in' retirement communities where everyone shares a little airport and all the houses have hangers instead of garages. Intentional communities don't need to economically rationalize what they do. If a community decides Mars needs women, and there's enough of them to create the means to do it, they can do it. It's their own time, skill, and money. They can do what they want with it. But government and business isn't going to help, so your community better be big, well-heeled, and coherent. Unfortunately, you don't hear or see anyone in the space establishment or space advocacy talking about intentional communities (well, other than me...) because they don't get that concept. There's a strong undercurrent of Objectivism in the space establishment and Objectivists don't believe in community or any such thing as social responsibility. So they won't community-stead. The concept is as alien to them as Mars itself. They'll futilely chase the fantasy of Galt's Gulch in space.

I used to have hope in the potential creation of intentional communities for space development, but lately I've become resigned to the notion that we've probably already relegated the stars to our electric children. Space development driven by economic Darwinism--survival of the most cost-efficient--means space belongs to the artilects and unless we figure out how to join them--become them so we can travel like them--we're going there as tourists, traveling in their wake at their convenience. I don't see that as necessarily bad, but it's a picture of the future in space very different from anything SciFi or the space establishment has ever tried to illustrate for us.
